judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the viability of forming giant planets via gravitational fragmentation in the inner regions (<50 AU) of protostellar discs around solar-type stars. Using advanced Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations with a newly developed radiative transfer scheme, the authors model the thermodynamics of discs under two scenarios: one with only a low background radiation field (10 K) and another including heating from the central star. The simulations reveal that while discs can become gravitationally unstable (Toomre Q < 1) in the background-only case, they fail to fragment because the cooling timescale exceeds the dynamical timescale (t_COOL > 2 t_ORB). Conversely, when stellar irradiation is included, the disc remains thermally stable (Q > 1.5) and does not fragment. These results corroborate previous analytic and numerical studies suggesting that efficient cooling mechanisms are absent in the inner disc regions, thereby ruling out gravitational fragmentation as a primary formation mechanism for hot Jupiters at close orbital distances. The work highlights the critical role of radiative transfer treatments in determining disc stability and planetary formation pathways.

Research Context
Disc fragmentation is a proposed mechanism for giant planet formation. The mechanism requires rapid cooling on a dynamical timescale. Previous studies yield contradictory results regarding inner disc stability. Discrepancies arise from differing treatments of radiative transfer. Analytic studies suggest convection cannot provide required cooling.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to investigate the thermodynamics of discs. The central question is whether fragmentation can function in the inner region. Hypothesis 1: A disc heated only by a 10 K background field will fragment. Hypothesis 2: A disc heated by the central star will fragment. The authors predict fragmentation is unlikely due to cooling inefficiency. Stellar irradiation is hypothesized to stabilize the disc against fragmentation.

Methodological Details
The study uses SPH simulations of protostellar discs. A newly developed method treats the energy equation and equation of state. The method accounts for radiative transfer effects in the simulations. Chemical states of hydrogen and dust properties are included. The simulations focus on the inner parts of discs with R < 40 AU. Two cases are examined: background heating and stellar heating. The code used is the SPH code dragon. The gas is assumed to be a mixture of hydrogen and helium. Opacity changes due to ice melting and dust sublimation are taken into account. The disc initially extends from 2 to 40 AU. The initial surface density follows a profile of Sigma(R) ~ R^-1/2. The initial temperature follows a profile of T(R) ~ R^-1. 2 x 10^5 SPH particles are used to represent the disc.

Procedures And Architectures
The energy equation includes compressional, viscous, and radiation heating. Radiation cooling is implicitly treated via the particle's neighbourhood. The equation of state includes rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom. The equation of state includes H2 dissociation and He ionization effects. Opacity is parameterized by Bell & Lin (1994) as kappa(rho, T) = kappa0 rho^a T^b. The code reproduces detailed 3D results of Masunaga & Inutsuka (2000). Simulation 1 uses a constant background radiation field of TBGR = 10 K. Simulation 2 uses radiation from the central star with TBGR ~ R^-1. The disc relaxes to a quasi-steady state within ~250 yr in the first case. The adiabatic index gamma is 5/3 outside ~10 AU. Closer to the star, gamma is 7/5 due to rotational excitation.

Key Results
In the background heating case, the disc does not fragment. The disc cannot cool fast enough in the background heating scenario. Cooling time throughout the disc is generally >~2 t_ORB. Weak spiral arms form but show no tendency to fragment. The disc is Toomre unstable at ~30-35 AU in the background case. In the stellar heating case, the disc is not gravitationally unstable. The Toomre parameter Q is >~1.5 K in the stellar heating case. The disc appears axisymmetric with no signs of spiral arms. Temperatures calculated are ~15% higher than Boley et al. (2006). Temperatures are less than 3% higher than Cai et al. (2007). Vertical temperature profiles match Hubeny (1990) analytic calculations. Disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets at radii <~50 AU.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Fragmentation requires both gravitational instability and fast cooling. The cooling condition t_COOL < C(gamma) t_ORB is not met in the inner disc. Stellar irradiation stabilizes the disc by increasing temperature. Higher temperatures increase the Toomre parameter Q. Higher temperatures decrease the cooling time t_COOL. Results agree with analytic studies that convection cannot provide cooling. Planetary mass objects forming at large radii are unlikely to migrate inwards. Hot Jupiters probably cannot form close to the star by fragmentation.

Contradictions And Limitations
Hydrodynamic simulations have produced contradictory results. Discrepancies are attributable to different background radiation fields. Discrepancies may be due to higher viscous heating in the current simulations. Contributions from metals are ignored in the equation of state. The mean molecular weight mu is assumed constant. Temperatures are not high enough for molecular hydrogen to dissociate. The study focuses only on the inner disc region R < 40 AU. Fragmentation at large radii might produce brown dwarfs or low-mass stars.

Claims
Gravitational fragmentation cannot form giant planets in the inner disc region (<50 AU) due to inefficient cooling and stellar stabilization. disc does not fragment; in the former case because it cannot cool fast enough disc does not fragment because it is not gravitationally unstable disc fragmentation is unlikely to be able to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii <~50 AU Hydrodynamic simulations have produced contradictory results about whether disc fragmentation can produce giant planets close to the central star 
Radiative transfer treatments significantly impact predicted disc stability and fragmentation outcomes. reported discrepancies are rather small despite using different treatments for the radiative transfer and for the hydrodynamics The spiral arms that develop in the disc are weaker than those reported by Boley et al. (2006) 

Data And Code Availability
Computations were performed using the UK Astrophysical Fluids Facility (UKAFF).

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The simulation was repeated using a smaller number of SPH particles (5 x 10^4). The evolution of thermal energy, surface density, temperature, Toomre parameter and cooling time were essentially the same.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1 shows the evolution of the disc internal energy with time for both cases. Fig. 2 shows logarithmic column density and cross-section of the density for the background heating case. Fig. 4 shows the Toomre parameter in the x-y plane for the background heating case. Fig. 5 shows the cooling time in units of the local orbital period for the background heating case. Fig. 11 shows the Toomre parameter for the disc heated by the central star. Fig. 12 shows the cooling time for the disc heated by the central star.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that inner discs do not fragment due to inefficient cooling and stellar heating. 2. The strongest evidence is the quantitative comparison of cooling times and Toomre parameters showing stability. 3. The future path involves investigating fragmentation at larger radii where cooling times are sufficiently short.
